subtitle: The idea fits in one sentence, and it scales to large datasets.

steps.label: 1-2: PICK k CENTERS, ASSIGN EACH ROW
3-4: MOVE CENTROID TO THE MEAN, REPEAT

eyebrow: Running it: inertia is what k-means minimizes
code:
km = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init="k-means++", n_init=10).fit(Xs)
print(round(km.inertia_, 2), km.n_iter_)
# 52.37  2
caption: Each pass can only LOWER the total squared distance -- the loop always settles.

eyebrow: Centers back in business units, and predicting new rows
caption: Always apply the SAME fitted scaler to new data -- never a fresh one.

eyebrow: A bad start can trap the loop
code:
for seed in range(4):
    k1 = KMeans(n_clusters=3, init="random", n_init=1, random_state=seed).fit(Xs)
    print(seed, round(k1.inertia_, 2))
# 0: 52.37   1: 334.76 (!)   2: 52.37   3: 52.37
caption: Seed 1 gets stuck 6x worse -- just from a different random starting point.

steps.label: n_init: RERUN, KEEP THE BEST
steps.sub: Set it explicitly -- defaults vary by version

caption: Real output: k-means draws straight boundaries -- it cuts each crescent right in half.
